attention.question: Find the animal hidden among the trees.
attention.hint: Look for something that isn't a tree.

attention.question: Find the bird hidden in the clouds.
attention.hint: There's only one element that's different.

attention.question: Find the donut among the cookies.
attention.hint: It has a hole in the middle.

attention.question: Find the car that's different from the others.
attention.hint: It's a bit taller than the others.

errors.scenario: Tom tried to stack the blocks, but the tower fell when he put the bigger block on top.
reflectionPrompts: What do you think happened to the tower?
What could Tom try next time?
Do you think trying again can help you learn?

errors.scenario: Ines tried to draw a cat, but the ears came out too big and she didn't like the result.
reflectionPrompts: What did Ines learn about drawing ears?
What could she do differently in the next drawing?
Do you think artists also make drawings they don't like at first?

errors.scenario: Rui added 3 + 4 and said it was 6, but the correct answer was actually 7.
reflectionPrompts: Where do you think Rui might have miscounted?
What strategy could he use to check the sum?
What does this mistake show us we can still practise?

errors.scenario: Diogo tried to ride a bike without training wheels and fell right after he started pedalling.
reflectionPrompts: What do you think Diogo's body was learning as he fell?
What could he try to hold onto better next time?
Do you think people who ride well ever fell while learning?

errors.scenario: Maria told the teacher that the capital of Portugal was Porto, but the right answer was Lisbon.
reflectionPrompts: Why do you think she might have mixed up the cities?
How can Maria remember the right answer better?
Does one wrong answer mean we know nothing?

errors.scenario: Pedro tried to do a puzzle and put a piece in the wrong spot several times.
reflectionPrompts: What might Pedro have discovered about the piece's shape?
What other way of looking at the piece could help?
Do you think trying different pieces is a good way to learn?

errors.scenario: Miguel wrote the word 'gato' (cat) as 'gatu' in his notebook.
reflectionPrompts: Which sound do you think Miguel mixed up?
How can he check the word next time?
What does this kind of mistake teach us about vowels?

errors.scenario: Sofia tried to sing a new song and swapped the order of two parts of the lyrics.
reflectionPrompts: What do you think would help Sofia remember the right order?
Do you think singing it again, more slowly, could help?
Is it normal to make mistakes when learning something new?

errors.scenario: Tiago tried to build a tower of cards, but it fell as soon as he touched the last card.
reflectionPrompts: What do you think made the tower fall this time?
What could Tiago change about how he places the cards?
How do you feel when something you try doesn't work right away?

errors.scenario: Andre picked the shortest path on the treasure map, but that path actually had a river in the middle.
reflectionPrompts: What did Andre learn about looking closely at the map?
What could he do before choosing the path next time?
Can a path that doesn't work still teach us something?

errors.scenario: Bia tried to read the word 'igreja' (church) out loud, but mixed up the 'g' sound and said it wrong.
reflectionPrompts: Which sound do you think Bia mixed up?
How can she practise that sound again?
Does reading out loud help us notice our own mistakes?

errors.scenario: Nuno tried to subtract 12 - 5 and said it was 8, but the correct answer was 7.
reflectionPrompts: Where do you think Nuno miscounted?
What strategy could he use to check the sum?
Can checking our sums again help us learn?

errors.scenario: Gustavo built a Lego garage, but the roof collapsed because the walls were too thin.
reflectionPrompts: Why do you think the roof fell this time?
What could Gustavo change about the walls?
Is testing and rebuilding a good way to learn to build things?

errors.scenario: Carolina said without meaning to that her friend's drawing was ugly, and her friend felt sad.
reflectionPrompts: How do you think Carolina's friend felt?
What could Carolina say to show she's sorry?
What do we learn when our words hurt someone without meaning to?

errors.scenario: Vasco moved his board game piece two spaces instead of three and had to move back.
reflectionPrompts: What do you think Vasco forgot to do before playing?
How can he pay more attention to his next move?
Can reading the rules carefully before starting help?

errors.scenario: Bruno predicted the plant would grow faster in the shade, but it actually grew more in the sun.
reflectionPrompts: What did Bruno learn from this experiment?
Do wrong predictions in science also teach us something?
How could he test it again to be sure?

errors.scenario: Leonor played the wrong note in the middle of a piano piece and had to stop.
reflectionPrompts: What do you think would help Leonor get the note right?
Can playing more slowly help us learn a piece of music?
Do musicians also hit wrong notes while practising?

errors.scenario: Simao took a shot at goal in football, but the ball flew over the crossbar.
reflectionPrompts: What could Simao adjust for his next shot?
Does missing a shot mean he plays badly?
How would you feel about trying again right away?

strategy.prompt: How can you cross the river without getting your feet wet?
strategy.firstTry: You tried jumping from stone to stone, but one of the stones wobbles a lot.
strategy.hint1: What if you asked someone who already knows the way for help?
strategy.hint2: What if you looked for a bridge a bit further along?
strategy.answer: You could look for a bridge, ask someone for help, or build a small path with extra stones.

strategy.prompt: How can you open a jar whose lid is very tight?
strategy.firstTry: You tried turning the lid with your hands, but it wouldn't loosen.
strategy.hint1: What if you used a cloth to get a better grip?
strategy.hint2: What if you asked an adult for help?
strategy.answer: You could use a cloth for grip, run the lid under warm water, or ask for help.

strategy.prompt: How can you reach a book on a high shelf?
strategy.firstTry: You tried stretching your arm as far as you could, but you couldn't reach it.
strategy.hint1: What if you used a safe little stool to climb up?
strategy.hint2: What if you asked someone taller to help?
strategy.answer: You could use a safe stool, ask someone taller for help, or use a long stick carefully.

strategy.prompt: How can you find out how many marbles fit in a jar without counting them one by one?
strategy.firstTry: You tried counting one by one, but lost count halfway through.
strategy.hint1: What if you counted them in groups of 10 instead of one by one?
strategy.hint2: What if you asked someone to count along with you?
strategy.answer: You could count in groups (of 5 or 10), ask for help, or split the marbles into smaller piles.

strategy.prompt: How can you set up a camping tent by yourself?
strategy.firstTry: You tried going from memory, but the poles didn't fit together well.
strategy.hint1: What if you looked for the instructions that came with the tent?
strategy.hint2: What if you asked someone to hold one part while you set up the other?
strategy.answer: You could read the instructions calmly, ask for help, or set it up piece by piece.

strategy.prompt: How can you remember to bring everything you need for school tomorrow?
strategy.firstTry: You tried relying only on memory, but forgot your lunch.
strategy.hint1: What if you made a list and checked it before leaving?
strategy.hint2: What if you packed your bag the night before, calmly?
strategy.answer: You could make a list, pack the bag the night before, or ask someone to help you check.

strategy.prompt: How can you settle an argument with a friend about which game to play?
strategy.firstTry: You tried insisting only on your favourite game, but your friend got upset.
strategy.hint1: What if you suggested playing one game today and another tomorrow?
strategy.hint2: What if you used a simple draw, like odds or evens?
strategy.answer: You could take turns choosing games, draw lots, or find a third game you both like.

strategy.prompt: How can you make a tower of blocks taller without it falling?
strategy.firstTry: You tried stacking everything quickly, but the tower fell before you finished.
strategy.hint1: What if you put the bigger blocks at the bottom and smaller ones on top?
strategy.hint2: What if you built more slowly, checking the balance with each block?
strategy.answer: You could put bigger blocks at the base, build slowly, or make the base wider.

strategy.prompt: How can you decorate a drawing in a different way than you've done before?
strategy.firstTry: You tried using the same colours as always, but wanted something different.
strategy.hint1: What if you tried a colour you've never used for this kind of drawing?
strategy.hint2: What if you asked someone for an idea and mixed it with your own?
strategy.answer: You could try new colours, ask someone for ideas, or mix two different styles.

strategy.prompt: How can you memorise a short poem you're learning for school?
strategy.firstTry: You tried reading the poem once and reciting it, but forgot half of it.
strategy.hint1: What if you split the poem into small parts and learned one at a time?
strategy.hint2: What if you said the poem out loud several times instead of reading it silently?
strategy.answer: You could learn it in parts, repeat it out loud, or ask someone to listen to you say it.

strategy.prompt: How can you get a big box through a narrow door?
strategy.firstTry: You tried pushing the box straight through, but it won't fit through the door.
strategy.hint1: What if you turned the box sideways to make it narrower?
strategy.hint2: What if you took a few things out of the box first?
strategy.answer: You could turn the box sideways, empty it a bit, or ask for help tilting it carefully.

strategy.prompt: How can you find out which number your friend is thinking of, between 1 and 20?
strategy.firstTry: You tried guessing random numbers, but haven't gotten it right yet.
strategy.hint1: What if you asked whether the number is higher or lower than 10?
strategy.hint2: What if you kept splitting the range in half with each question?
strategy.answer: You could ask 'higher or lower', keep splitting the range in half, or ask for an extra clue.

strategy.prompt: How can you make cookies by following the right steps?
strategy.firstTry: You tried mixing everything at once, but the dough came out strange.
strategy.hint1: What if you looked at the recipe and followed one step at a time?
strategy.hint2: What if you separated the dry ingredients from the wet ones first?
strategy.answer: You could follow the recipe step by step, separate ingredients first, or ask an adult to check each stage.

strategy.prompt: How can you find the shortest path in a maze drawn on paper?
strategy.firstTry: You tried following the first path you saw, but it ended in a dead end.
strategy.hint1: What if you started from the end of the maze and worked backwards?
strategy.hint2: What if you used your finger to mark the paths you've already tried?
strategy.answer: You could start from the end and work backwards, mark paths you've tried, or calmly rule out dead ends first.

strategy.prompt: How can you figure out which of these objects doesn't belong in the group?
strategy.firstTry: You tried looking at the colours, but they all seemed to fit somehow.
strategy.hint1: What if you thought about the size of each object instead of the colour?
strategy.hint2: What if you thought about what each object is used for?
strategy.answer: You could compare size, shape, or use of each object to find the one that doesn't belong.

strategy.prompt: How can you get dressed in the right order on a very cold day?
strategy.firstTry: You tried putting your coat on first, but then couldn't fit the jumper on underneath.
strategy.hint1: What if you thought about what goes closest to your body first?
strategy.hint2: What if you imagined the layers like an onion, from the inside out?
strategy.answer: You could put on what's closest to your skin first, then the middle layers, and the coat last.

strategy.prompt: How can you arrange the furniture in your playroom so it isn't too cramped?
strategy.firstTry: You tried placing everything wherever it fit, but then there was no room to walk.
strategy.hint1: What if you drew a small map of the room first?
strategy.hint2: What if you placed the bigger furniture first and the small pieces around it?
strategy.answer: You could draw a plan first, place bigger furniture first, or measure the free space before deciding.

strategy.prompt: How can you find out which of two toys is heavier without a scale?
strategy.firstTry: You tried guessing just by looking, but weren't sure.
strategy.hint1: What if you held one in each hand to feel the weight?
strategy.hint2: What if you used a ruler balanced on a pencil as a makeshift scale?
strategy.answer: You could compare the weight in your hands, use a makeshift balance, or ask an adult for a kitchen scale.

teachback.concept: Why does saying something out loud help us remember?
options: Because speaking loudly scares forgetting away.
Because hearing and saying it at the same time gives our brain two ways to store the information.
Because it's more fun to shout.

teachback.concept: Why does paying attention to an important detail help us solve problems?
options: Because the right detail gives us the clue we need to understand the rest.
Because looking closely tires the eyes less.
Because details are always the prettiest part.

teachback.concept: Why do mistakes help us learn?
options: Because making a mistake shows us exactly what we don't know yet, so we can practise it.
Because mistakes are always someone else's fault.
Because whoever makes a mistake has to stop trying.

teachback.concept: Why is it worth trying another strategy when one doesn't work?
options: Because giving up is always the fastest option.
Because no strategy ever really works.
Because a problem can often be solved in more than one good way.

teachback.concept: Why does explaining something to a friend help us learn better?
options: Because explaining forces us to organise the ideas in our head.
Because talking a lot tires the throat.
Because friends always like hearing stories.

teachback.concept: Why does grouping information into small chunks help memory?
options: Because small groups are easier to hold onto than one long list all at once.
Because the brain only likes even numbers.
Because grouping makes everything more colourful.

teachback.concept: Why does practising again after a mistake usually work better?
options: Because repeating without thinking always guarantees success.
Because we already know what didn't work, so we can adjust our next try.
Because the second try is always easier by luck.

teachback.concept: Why is asking questions about a mistake better than just saying 'wrong'?
options: Because questions help us think about what happened and figure out the solution ourselves.
Because questions make the mistake disappear.
Because it's quicker than explaining.

teachback.concept: Why does sounding out the letters of a word help us read it?
options: Because joining each sound helps us work out the whole word, step by step.
Because letters like being said out loud.
Because sounding it out makes the word shorter.

teachback.concept: Why is it a good idea to check our maths sum again?
options: Because checking tires the brain, so we learn more.
Because checking again helps us find mistakes we didn't notice the first time.
Because the second sum is always the right one.

teachback.concept: Why does making a prediction before a science experiment help us learn?
options: Because predicting makes the experiment faster.
Because comparing what we predicted with what actually happened helps us understand the result better.
Because predictions are always correct.

teachback.concept: Why does practising writing a word several times help us write it correctly?
options: Because writing a lot tires the hand, so we stop making mistakes.
Because practising helps our brain remember the correct shape of the word.
Because the last time we write it is always the best, by luck.

teachback.concept: Why can drawing a maths problem help us solve it?
options: Because drawing is always more fun than counting.
Because a drawing shows the problem visually, making it easier to see what to do.
Because drawing replaces the need to think.

teachback.concept: Why does asking 'why' help us understand science better?
options: Because asking 'why' makes us look for the reason behind what we observe.
Because asking a lot tires the teacher out.
Because questions make the topic disappear.

teachback.concept: Why does re-reading a sentence we didn't understand help us understand the story?
options: Because re-reading gives us another chance to notice words or ideas we missed.
Because re-reading makes the story shorter.
Because the second reading is always exactly the same as the first.

teachback.concept: Why does using fingers or objects to count help when we're learning maths?
options: Because counting with objects makes numbers more concrete and easier to picture.
Because fingers always know the right answer.
Because counting with objects is slower, so it's better.

teachback.concept: Why does observing carefully help us make discoveries in science?
options: Because observing well helps us notice details that might explain what's happening.
Because observing replaces the experiment.
Because whoever observes fastest always discovers the most.

teachback.concept: Why does retelling a story in our own words help us understand what we read better?
options: Because summarising in our own words shows us whether we really understood the story.
Because retelling makes the story longer.
Because our own words are always better than the book's.
